title: Stories from Before the Republic
subtitle: Fragments of older Vesperian belief
summary: Fairy tales that may be fossils of prayers, festival masks nobody can explain, and customs kept because a grandmother kept them.
content:
> *"It's not religious. My grandmother did it."*
> — a common Vesperian answer, to which folklorists rarely agree

Vesper has broken with its past more deliberately than almost any country in the world. Religious reforms, political revolutions, secular movements and modernisation campaigns have each, in turn, set out to sweep something old away. Much of what came before the [[sacred-flame|Sacred Flame]] was abolished, marginalised, absorbed into later faith, or simply stripped of its meaning.

What remains is a scatter of **fragments**: fairy tales, urban legends, children's stories, festival customs, masks, place names, household sayings, rural superstitions and architectural symbols that nobody can explain any more. Many Vesperians keep these customs without a second thought. Very few could tell you what they once meant.

No one has reconstructed the older Vesperian religion, and this entry does not try to. It collects what survives, and what scholars suspect about it. Treat everything here as fragmentary, local and disputed.

## What Was Lost

It seems likely that some Vesperian folk stories once concerned divine or spiritual figures. Their names, and whatever roles they once had, are lost. Some were taken up and reinterpreted by the First Light. Others were reduced, during the revolutionary years, to stories for children. A few may survive only as a figure on a festival float or a face carved over a doorway.

There is no recovered pantheon, no agreed cosmology and no list of old gods. Anyone in Endros who claims to know the names of the old Vesperian gods is selling something, usually a book.

## Fairy Tales as Fossils

Some Vesperian folklorists argue that several well-loved children's stories are fossils of older religious practice: tales that keep the shape of a prayer or a rite long after anyone stopped praying it. It is a scholarly argument, not a settled fact, and the folklorists argue with each other about it at least as much as with anyone else.

> **From a historian's letter to a colleague**
>
> *I was staying with my sister's family, and her mother-in-law was putting the youngest to bed with "The Girl Who Kept the Lamp", the one every child knows. I was barely listening.*
>
> *Then she came to the line where the girl stands at the threshold and says, "I am here, and I am awake, and the door is mine." She said it in the old way, with the pause after "awake".*
>
> *You will remember the inscription from the shrine at the old ford, the one we could never translate past the third word. I am almost certain it is the same line. I asked her where she had learned it. She said, "From my grandmother, obviously. It's just a story."*
>
> *I have not slept much since.*

## Festivals and Masks

Vesperian festivals are full of actions people perform perfectly without knowing why: a particular mask worn on a particular night, a procession that takes an odd route through a town, something left on a doorstep, a lamp lit at an exact hour, branches or ribbons carried and then left somewhere specific. Participants know precisely **how** a custom is done. The **why** has gone.

Some festivals have been reinterpreted through the Sacred Flame, some through revolutionary symbolism, and some through nothing at all. Several of them have been through all three, which can make them very confusing to watch.

> **Overheard at a spring festival in a market town**
>
> "Why the hare mask?"
>
> The young man adjusting it looked genuinely surprised by the question.
>
> "Because you wear the hare mask on the first night."
>
> "Yes, but why a hare?"
>
> He thought about it for a while.
>
> "My father wore one. His father wore one. There's a hare carved over the old well, too." He shrugged and pulled the mask down. "I suppose somebody knew, once."

## Small Survivals

Older belief also survives in smaller ways:

- **Household sayings** whose literal meaning makes no sense, but which everybody uses.
- **Place names** for hills, springs, bridges and crossroads that seem once to have had a religious meaning nobody now remembers.
- **Architectural symbols** carved on older buildings: faces, animals and patterns that later builders copied faithfully without knowing what they meant.
- **Rural superstitions**, kept mostly by farmers and sailors, and mostly denied by their grandchildren.

Most Vesperians take a cheerfully practical attitude to all of this. If a custom is pleasant, they keep it. If someone asks what it means, they tell them it isn't religious, their grandmother did it. The folklorists, who know very well that the grandmother's grandmother might have had a different answer, write it down.

## What This Means Now

Vesper's relationship with its own past is complicated. The Republic is proud of having remade itself, and wary of anyone who wants to bring the old order back. At the same time, more and more Vesperians, especially since the Gates appeared, find themselves curious about what was lost.

For now, the older Vesperian beliefs remain what they have been for generations: fragments, half-remembered, in stories and festivals, waiting for someone to work out what they were. The Archive will record more as more is found.
